absent: Big-block unplug request path and online versus offline handling for big blocks.
Locking and concurrency rules for plugged_size, request and response storage, and queue access.
Numeric values and wire layout of request and response structures and response codes.
Removal and device-teardown race handling referenced by the online callback.
Meaning and control of the flag disabling online unplug.

findings.text: Fake offline attempts a bounded retry loop of five tries. Each iteration first checks a config-changed flag and aborts when set, then attempts a contiguous allocation over the target range. Out-of-memory ends immediately, failure on non-movable range ends the loop, failure on movable range retries, and success marks the range fake offline, decrements managed count, and reports success; exhaustion reports busy.

Page onlining distinguishes sub-block mode from big-block mode. Sub-block mode maps each covered address range to memory-block and sub-block identifiers, checks whether the covered sub-blocks are fully plugged, fully unplugged, or mixed, and on mixed input narrows granularity to sub-block size exactly once before continuing. Big-block mode checks one big-block state. Plugged ranges go through generic onlining, unplugged ranges are left fake offline.

A global page-online callback scans registered devices for the one containing the page range, drops RCU protection before invoking the per-device online routine because that path may sleep and removal is handled elsewhere, and falls back to generic onlining when no device contains the range.

Host requests are issued by copying a caller request into device storage, building one outbound and one inbound scatter element for request and response, adding them to the device queue, kicking the queue, waiting for completion, then interpreting the response type after endian conversion.

Plug requests refuse work when configuration changed, derive block count from size divided by device block size, and update accounting only on acknowledgement by adding size to plugged total. Negative responses map to retry, busy, invalid, or no-memory outcomes.

Unplug requests similarly refuse work when configuration changed, derive block count from size, subtract size from plugged total only on acknowledgement, and map busy and error responses to corresponding failures. Unplug-all clears plugged total and the unplug-all-required flag on acknowledgement and raises config-changed because usable range may have shrunk.

Sub-block plug and unplug compute address as memory-block base plus sub-block index times sub-block size, and size as count times sub-block size. Bitmap state is updated to plugged or unplugged only when the host request succeeds.
Big-block plug and unplug derive address from big-block identifier and use configured big-block size for the host request.

Raw sub-block unplug scans from the highest sub-block downward, skips already unplugged entries, coalesces downward contiguous plugged entries up to the remaining demand, issues one host request per coalesced run, and decrements remaining demand by the run length.

Preparing the next memory or big block fails when the next identifier exceeds the last usable identifier, grows persistent state structures first, increments the unused counter, publishes the identifier, and advances the next counter.

Plug-and-add plugs before exposing memory to Linux. Sub-block mode plugs a bounded prefix of sub-blocks, marks the block offline or partially offline according to full or partial coverage, then adds it; on add failure it attempts unplug and records unused on success or plugged on failure. Big-block mode requires unused state, plugs, marks added, then adds, reverting to unused when compensating unplug succeeds and to plugged otherwise.

Plugging into an existing sub-block memory block repeatedly finds the first unplugged sub-block, extends over following unplugged entries up to remaining demand, plugs the run, and when the block was already online returns those pages to the allocator. If all sub-blocks end plugged, the block state is moved one step from its prior partial state toward the corresponding whole state.

Sub-block plug demand is expressed in sub-blocks. Partial kernel, partial movable, then partial offline blocks are filled first while holding the hotplug mutex; the mutex is then released before handling unused blocks and newly prepared blocks, each guarded by a capacity check and cooperative rescheduling.

Big-block plug demand is expressed in big blocks. Unused blocks are plugged and added first, then new blocks are prepared, plugged, and added, each step guarded by capacity checks and cooperative rescheduling; remaining demand is decremented only on success.
Top-level plug dispatch selects sub-block or big-block handling according to a mode flag.

Unplugging from offline sub-block memory delegates to raw unplug, marks the block partially offline when no plugged sub-block remains even on failure, and when every sub-block is unplugged marks the block unused, temporarily releases the hotplug mutex while removing it from Linux, then reacquires the mutex; removal is treated as infallible.

Unplugging from online sub-block memory first fake-offlines the page range, then requests host unplug, and on host failure returns pages to the allocator. On success a whole kernel or movable block transitions to the corresponding partial state.

Online sub-block unplug prefers one whole-block attempt when demand covers the block and the block is fully plugged; only busy falls back to descending single-sub-block attempts that skip unplugged entries, ignore busy per entry, and abort other errors. Afterwards it attempts removal of a fully unplugged block and records a pending-removal flag on failure while reporting success.

Sub-block unplug dispatch routes kernel, movable, and their partial states to the online path, offline and partially offline states to the offline path, and rejects unknown states. The request path visits offline-partial, offline, movable-partial, kernel-partial, movable, then kernel in reverse order, drops and reacquires the mutex around rescheduling, stops after offline states when online unplug is disabled, and reports busy when demand remains.

Observed sub-block memory-block states include unused, offline, offline-partial, kernel, kernel-partial, movable, movable-partial, and plugged. Plug moves partial toward whole and creates offline or offline-partial for newly added blocks; unplug moves whole online toward partial and fully unplugged offline toward unused or offline-partial; add failure can leave plugged.

Observed big-block states include unused, plugged, and added. Normal plug-and-add moves unused through plugged to added; compensating unplug after add failure returns to unused when it succeeds and remains plugged when it fails.

A per-device hotplug mutex serializes sub-block plug and unplug against memory onlining and offlining. It is held while iterating online, offline, and partial blocks, released before operating on unused or new blocks in the plug path, and temporarily released around removal and around rescheduling in unplug paths; state changes during release are handled by later retries.

The global device list is traversed under RCU read protection when locating the device owning an onlining range; the lock is released before calling into the device online path because that path may sleep.

Observed device state includes a sub-block versus big-block mode selector, queue and embedded request and response storage, a host-response wait object, an atomic config-changed flag, plugged-size and unplug-all-required fields, a hotplug mutex, and sub-block or big-block descriptors holding element size, counts, next and last usable identifiers, and state tables.

Host request submission waits for a host response and therefore must not run in atomic context. Long plug and unplug scans yield the processor and may observe state changes while the mutex is dropped. Block removal after full offline unplug is asserted to succeed.
Host protocol uses distinct plug, unplug, and unplug-all request types and acknowledgement, negative acknowledgement, busy, and error response types that drive accounting and error mapping.
